title: Arrays: Left Rotation
directAnswer: Left-rotating by d moves each element d slots toward the front, wrapping around. The naive O(n·d) shifts one step at a time. The clean O(n) answer is pure index math: element originally at index i lands at (i - d) mod n, or equivalently the new array's position i holds the old element at (i + d) mod n. For O(1) extra space, use the three-reversal trick: reverse [0, d), reverse [d, n), then reverse the whole array.

remember.pattern: Modular index remap + three-reversal in-place rotation
remember.formula:
# new array via index math
result[(i - d) % n] = a[i]   # element at i goes here
# or, fill destination directly:
result[i] = a[(i + d) % n]

# in-place three reversals (left rotate by d):
reverse(a, 0, d - 1)
reverse(a, d, n - 1)
reverse(a, 0, n - 1)
rules: Always reduce the shift first: `d %= n`. A rotation by `n` (or any multiple) is the identity — skip the work and avoid mod-by-zero style bugs.
Left rotation: the element at old index `i` moves to `(i - d + n) % n`; equivalently new position `i` pulls from old `(i + d) % n`. Pick one convention and stay consistent.
The `+ n` before `% n` matters in languages where `%` can go negative (Java) — Python's `%` is already non-negative.
The three-reversal trick rotates **in place** in O(1) extra space: reverse the first `d`, reverse the rest, reverse everything.
Left rotate by `d` and right rotate by `n - d` are the same operation — a common source of off-by-direction bugs.
whenToUse: Cyclically shift / rotate an array or string by a fixed offset
Wrap-around indexing problems ('the next element after the last is the first')
In-place rotation under an O(1) extra-space constraint → reversal trick
Any time you catch yourself shifting elements one at a time in a loop
antiSignals: You only need to *read* rotated values, not materialize them → just index with (i + d) % n on the fly, no copy
Rotation amount changes every query → precompute or use a deque/offset pointer instead of physically moving data
Data is a linked list, not an array → relink nodes instead of index math
remember.takeaway: Rotation is modular arithmetic in disguise: every element's destination is a simple (i ± d) mod n. Once you see that, you never shift one-at-a-time again — you either remap into a new array in O(n) or do the three-reversal dance in place. The same wrap-around index trick powers circular buffers, Rotate Array, and string rotation checks.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can express a rotation as a closed-form modular index map instead of repeated single-step shifts, and whether you know the in-place three-reversal technique for the O(1)-space variant.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: O(n·d) one-step-at-a-time shifting (times out for large d), forgetting d %= n, or getting the sign wrong so you right-rotate instead of left-rotate.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the index formula out loud, reduce d %= n first, then offer the three-reversal in-place method for O(1) space and explain why three reversals compose into a rotation.

problemStatement:
A left rotation operation on an array shifts each of the array's elements `1` unit to the left. For example, if `2` left rotations are performed on array `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, the array becomes `[3, 4, 5, 1, 2]`.

Given an array `a` of `n` integers and a number `d`, perform `d` left rotations on the array and return the resulting array.
understanding: Shift every element d positions toward index 0, with the first d elements wrapping around to the back. Position-wise, the new array is a[d], a[d+1], …, a[n-1], a[0], …, a[d-1]. The whole task is a cyclic relabeling of indices.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is d guaranteed to be ≤ n, or could it be larger?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Here d ≤ n, but you should still write d %= n defensively — rotating by n returns the array unchanged, and the mod makes any d work.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I have to rotate in place, or can I return a new array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Returning a new array is fine and simplest (O(n) space). If the interviewer demands O(1) extra space, switch to the three-reversal trick.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Left or right rotation?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Left: front elements move to the back. A left rotation by d equals a right rotation by n - d — worth confirming so you don't invert the direction.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain duplicates or negatives?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes; rotation is purely positional, so values are irrelevant to the logic.

examples.explanation: Each element moves 2 slots left; 1 and 2 wrap to the end.
Rotating by n (= 5) is a full cycle → unchanged. This is why d %= n matters.
A single left rotation swaps the two elements.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Rotate One Step at a Time
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to anchor the definition ('a left rotation shifts everything by one'), then immediately flag that repeating it d times is O(n·d) and won't scale.
hints: The problem defines a single left rotation: every element moves one slot left and the first element wraps to the back. Can you do exactly that once?
Save the first element, shift everything left by one, then place the saved element at the end.
Now repeat that single-rotation routine d times. What's the total cost?
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each single rotation shifts all n elements once → O(n). Doing it d times gives O(n·d). For n = 10⁵ and d near n that's ~10¹⁰ operations — far too slow.
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading of the prompt is 'perform d left rotations,' where one left rotation moves every element one slot toward the front. So implement a single rotation — stash `a[0]`, shift `a[1..n-1]` down into `a[0..n-2]`, drop the stashed value into `a[n-1]` — and run it `d` times.

**Why it's the natural first attempt.** It mirrors the problem statement one-to-one, so it's obviously correct and easy to reason about. Great for explaining *what* a rotation is.

**Why it doesn't scale.** Every single rotation touches all `n` elements, and you do that `d` times, so the cost is `O(n·d)`. When `d` is close to `n` (allowed by the constraints), that's quadratic — about `10¹⁰` operations at the limits, which times out. The deeper problem is that it re-moves the same elements over and over; after `d` rotations each element has been copied `d` times, when it only ever needed to move once. That waste is the cue to compute each element's *final* destination directly, which the optimal approaches do.
approaches.insight: Repeating a one-step operation d times almost always hides a closed-form shortcut. Here, an element rotated d times ends up exactly d slots left — so compute that final position once instead of stepping it there d times.

dryRun.intro: Apply a single left rotation twice.

java.explanation: Stash the front element before it gets overwritten by the shift.
Shift everything one slot left — the core of a single rotation.
Wrap the old front element around to the back.

python.explanation: Repeat a single rotation d times — this is the O(n·d) cost.
Save the element that wraps around this rotation.
Place the saved front element at the back.

pitfalls: Times out for large d — O(n·d) is quadratic when d ≈ n.
Overwriting arr[0] before stashing it, corrupting the shift.
Forgetting that d could equal n, doing a full pointless cycle instead of d %= n.

approaches.name: Index Math — Remap Into a New Array (Optimal, O(n) space)
approaches.whenToMention: The cleanest answer. Phrase it as 'each element's final index is a closed-form (i ± d) mod n, so I place it in one pass.'
hints: After d left rotations, where does the element originally at index i end up? It moves d slots left, wrapping around.
Old index i lands at (i - d + n) % n. Equivalently, new position i should hold the old element at (i + d) % n.
Reduce d %= n first, then fill a result array in a single pass with one of those formulas.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass computing one modular index and one assignment per element → O(n) time. The separate result array of size n → O(n) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Compute each element's destination directly and write it into a fresh array in one pass — no repeated shifting.

**Deriving the formula.** One left rotation sends index `i` to `i - 1` (mod n). Doing that `d` times sends `i` to `i - d` (mod n). To keep the index non-negative we write `(i - d + n) % n`. Equivalently, we can fill the destination directly: new position `i` should contain whatever ends up there, which is the old element at `(i + d) % n`. Both conventions describe the same rotation; pick one and apply it uniformly. The 'fill destination' form `result[i] = a[(i + d) % n]` is usually cleanest because the loop variable `i` indexes the output left to right.

**Why reduce `d %= n` first.** Rotating by `n` returns the original array, so only `d mod n` rotations are meaningful. Reducing up front avoids redundant arithmetic and guarantees the index stays in `[0, n)`. At the constraint `d ≤ n`, this also turns `d == n` into `d == 0` (a no-op) instead of a wasted full cycle.

**Why this is correct and fast.** Every element is read once and written exactly once to its final slot — no element moves twice. That's the whole improvement over brute force: we replaced `d` rounds of moving with one round of *computing where each element belongs*.

**The one cost.** It uses a second array of size `n`. If the interviewer forbids that, the three-reversal method below achieves the same rotation in place with `O(1)` extra space.
approaches.insight: Rotation is a relabeling of indices under addition mod n. Once you write the destination as a closed form, the loop becomes trivial and runs once. This 'compute the final position directly instead of simulating each step' move is the same insight behind fast modular exponentiation and any 'apply an operation k times' problem with a cyclic structure.

dryRun.intro: After d %= n (still 2), fill result[i] = a[(i + 2) % 5].

code.python:
def rotateLeft(self, d: int, a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(a)
    d %= n
    result: list[int] = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        result[i] = a[(i + d) % n]
    return result

java.explanation: Collapse full cycles — rotating by n or a multiple is a no-op.
Destination i pulls the old element d slots ahead, wrapping via % n.

python.explanation: Reduce the shift so the index stays in [0, n).
Each output slot directly grabs its source element — one pass, no shifting.

edgeCases.behavior: d %= 3 → 0, so result[i] = a[i] — the original array. Confirms full-cycle reduction.
n = 1, d %= 1 = 0 → unchanged single element. No mod-by-zero because n ≥ 1.

pitfalls: Skipping d %= n and indexing out of range when d ≥ n.
Mixing the two conventions: result[(i - d + n) % n] = a[i] and result[i] = a[(i + d) % n] are both correct, but blending them scrambles the array.
Right-rotating by using (i - d) when you meant a left rotation's (i + d) for the destination-fill form.

approaches.name: Three Reversals — In-Place Rotation (Optimal, O(1) space)
approaches.whenToMention: Bring this out when O(1) extra space is required. Explain why reversing the two halves then the whole array equals a rotation.
hints: Can you rotate without a second array? Think about what reversing sub-ranges does.
Reverse the first d elements, then reverse the remaining n - d elements.
Now reverse the entire array. The two halves swap places and each comes out in the correct order — that's a left rotation by d.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Three reversals touch a total of n + (something ≤ n) elements, each a constant-time swap → O(n) time. Reversals are done with two-pointer swaps in place → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Rotate in place using three in-bounds reversals, no auxiliary array.

**The construction.** A left rotation by `d` should produce `a[d..n-1]` followed by `a[0..d-1]`. The reversal trick builds exactly that: (1) reverse `a[0..d-1]`, (2) reverse `a[d..n-1]`, (3) reverse the whole array `a[0..n-1]`. 

**Why three reversals compose into a rotation.** Think of the array as two blocks `X = a[0..d-1]` and `Y = a[d..n-1]`; we want `Y X`. Reversing each block gives `Xᴿ Yᴿ`. Reversing the entire result flips the order of the two blocks *and* un-reverses each one: `(Xᴿ Yᴿ)ᴿ = (Yᴿ)ᴿ (Xᴿ)ᴿ = Y X`. That's precisely the rotated array. The double-reversal cancels within each block while the outer reversal swaps the blocks — elegant and exact.

**Why reduce `d %= n` first.** Same reason as before: a rotation by a multiple of `n` is the identity. Reducing also keeps the split point `d` inside the array so the sub-range reversals stay in bounds.

**Why O(1) space.** Each reversal is a two-pointer swap walking inward, mutating the array directly. No copy is made, so only a couple of index variables are used.
approaches.insight: Reversal is the secret weapon for in-place rearrangement: reversing parts and then the whole composes block swaps without extra memory. The identity `(Xᴿ Yᴿ)ᴿ = Y X` is worth memorizing — it turns 'rotate in place with O(1) space' from a puzzle into three lines. The same trick rotates strings and underlies Rotate Array (LeetCode 189).

dryRun.intro: Reverse [0,2), reverse [2,5), then reverse the whole array.

code.python:
def rotateLeft(self, d: int, a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    arr = a[:]
    n = len(arr)
    d %= n

    def reverse(lo: int, hi: int) -> None:
        while lo < hi:
            arr[lo], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[lo]
            lo += 1
            hi -= 1

    reverse(0, d - 1)
    reverse(d, n - 1)
    reverse(0, n - 1)
    return arr

java.explanation: Keep the split point inside the array and skip full cycles.
Reverse the first block X → Xᴿ.
Reverse the second block Y → Yᴿ.
Reverse everything: (Xᴿ Yᴿ)ᴿ = Y X, the rotated array.

python.explanation: Reduce the rotation amount before splitting.
Reverse the first d elements in place.
Reverse the remaining elements in place.
Final whole-array reverse swaps the two blocks into Y X.

diagrams.title: The three-reversal dance
diagrams.caption: Reverse first block, reverse second block, reverse the whole — blocks swap into place.

edgeCases.behavior: d %= 4 → 0. reverse(0,-1) is a no-op, reverse(0,3) then reverse(0,3) cancel → unchanged. Confirms d == n is the identity.
reverse [0,0) no-op, reverse [1,1) no-op, reverse [0,1) swaps → [8, 9]. Minimal rotation works.

pitfalls: Reversing the wrong sub-ranges or in the wrong order — only X then Y then whole yields a left rotation.
Off-by-one on the reverse bounds: use inclusive [d, n-1], not [d, n].
Forgetting d %= n so reverse(arr, 0, d-1) runs with d ≥ n and goes out of bounds.

commonMistakes: Shifting one element at a time d times — O(n·d) and times out for large d.
Forgetting d %= n, causing out-of-range indices or wasted full cycles.
Inverting the direction (right rotation) by adding when you should subtract, or vice versa.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Quadratic one-step shifting
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Calling a single-rotation routine d times copies every element d times. For d ≈ n that's O(n²) and times out. Compute the final index directly instead.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Negative modulo in Java
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Java's % returns a negative result for negative operands, so (i - d) % n can be negative and crash. Add n before the mod. (Python's % is already non-negative.)
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int dest = (i - d) % n;   // can be negative
result[dest] = arr[i];
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int dest = (i - d + n) % n;
result[dest] = arr[i];

patternNote: Modular Index Remap + Reversal Rotation. Recognise it on any cyclic shift: each element's destination is (i ± d) mod n, so either fill a new array in O(n) or rotate in place with three reversals in O(1) space. Always reduce d %= n first. Same shape as Rotate Array and Rotate String.
